scope: Documented cases in South Africa and elsewhere in Africa where a government (national, provincial, municipal) or government-contracted/partnered agency relocated, rehoused or accommodated displaced people (by floods, other disasters, conflict or evictions) in sites that were themselves flood-prone, and those sites later flooded or were officially or credibly assessed as flood-prone. Baseline for comparison: eThekwini's Lamontville temporary relocation area (TEA/TRA), April 2022 to February 2025.
method: Web search and page fetches carried out on 2026-09-27. Only facts found in accessed sources are recorded. Several primary documents could not be read directly: the Amnesty 'Flooded and Forgotten' PDF and the IOM DTM PDFs (no PDF text extraction was available), and ReliefWeb, some IOL and Citizen pages (HTTP 403). Where a fact comes from a search-engine summary or a secondary report of a primary document, the notes say so. Quotes are verbatim as returned by the fetch tool. Anything marked 'paraphrase' is not a verbatim quote. Victims are not named. 'not_found' means the sources accessed did not say. Confidence: high = several independent credible sources agree that the relocation was government-led AND the site flooded; medium = the site flooded or was assessed as flood-prone, but the government's role in choosing the site or the link to relocation is less direct or rests on one source; low = alleged, planned, or only loosely a relocation.

cases.place: Lamontville temporary relocation area (TRA/TEA), on the banks of the Umlazi (uMlazi) river, eThekwini (Durban), KwaZulu-Natal
cases.relocation_year: 2022 (after the April 2022 KZN floods). Some residents had already been moved in 2008 to the eMhlabeni transit camp in Lamontville after floods washed away their homes in uMlazi.
cases.reason_for_relocation: Households displaced by the April 2022 KwaZulu-Natal floods.
cases.floodprone_evidence: Later flood: the TRA flooded in February 2025 and five residents died. Amnesty International (Nov 2025) describes the TRA as 'on the banks of the Umlazi river'. Before that, the Auditor-General's 2022 real-time audit of KZN flood relief found that 20% of the 30 temporary residential units (TRUs) it inspected had been built on 'unsuitable land'. The brief describes this finding as units 'close to the riverbank'; that exact wording was not verified in the sources accessed. The South African Weather Service said of the area: 'The area is prone to flooding.'
cases.consequences: Five deaths in the TRA: two women aged 56 and 60, and three children aged 5, 11 and 16, according to Amnesty via IOL and Daily Maverick. Residents were displaced for the second time. About 280 families in Lamontville were affected and at least 40 families (nearly 230 people) were moved to a hotel. Amnesty via IOL says those accommodated in hotels were 'later evicted from a hotel after about 5 months'. Others were moved between Impala Holiday Flats and the Bayside Hotel. Relocation to the Cornubia housing project in Umhlanga met local opposition.
cases.deaths_at_site: 5 (per Amnesty International / IOL; Daily Maverick lists 5 Lamontville victims plus 1 in Chatsworth). One search-engine summary gave 7 deaths from a Lamontville transit camp; this was not verified.
cases.government_response: Mayor Cyril Xaba cited a lack of land and appealed to amakhosi (traditional leaders) to make land available, and attributed the damage to 'unprecedented rainfall'. The Premier, Thamsanqa Ntuli, called for urgent solutions. Human Settlements Minister Thembi Simelane promised temporary and permanent housing but said 'everyone might not qualify', and later described Umhlanga residents' opposition to resettling flood victims at Cornubia.
cases.risk_known_before: yes. (1) The camp area flooded in April 2022 and was publicly described as 'low-lying near the Umlaas Canal, which is prone to flooding' (Mail & Guardian op-ed, 9 May 2022). (2) The Auditor-General flagged in August 2022 that 20% of the TRUs inspected were on unsuitable land (this finding covers KZN TRUs generally, not necessarily this site). (3) An IOL Daily News headline (26 Feb 2025) refers to 'previous community warnings'; the article itself returned 403, so the content of those warnings was not verified.
cases.temporary_vs_permanent: Announced as a temporary relocation / temporary emergency accommodation area. Residents stayed about three years (2022 to Feb 2025). Some residents had been in Lamontville transit camps since 2008, about 17 years according to an IOL search snippet.
cases.distance_or_position: On the riverbank (banks of the Umlazi river), per Amnesty International.
cases.blame_framing: Weather and climate. Mayor Xaba spoke of 'unprecedented rainfall in recent years which has crippled key infrastructure like roads and bridges' (GroundUp). He also blamed land scarcity: 'We don't have enough land to settle people.' No official acceptance of responsibility for the site choice was found.
cases.warning_at_site: The South African Weather Service issued 'a Yellow Level 2 warning for the southern parts of KZN for severe thunderstorms' (Daily Maverick). Whether the warning reached TRA residents, and in what language (e.g. isiZulu), was not found.
cases.resident_voice: Yes, but limited in the sources accessed. Flood victims interviewed by IOL spoke mainly of looting of their belongings. An IOL headline reports a grieving mother calling for urgent relocation (not fetched).
cases.who_was_moved: Low-income residents of informal settlements in the uMlazi / Lamontville area of south Durban who had been displaced by floods; place-level only. Language or minority group: not_found.
cases.accountability_outcome: The Amnesty International report (Nov 2025) documented the case and found a 'serious failure to ensure that flood victims are relocated to safety'. No inquiry, court case, resignation or compensation specific to the site was found.

quotes.text: the City of eThekwini relocated around 100 flood-impacted households to a Temporary Relocation Area established in Lamontville, on the banks of the Umlazi river.
quotes.source: IOL, 19 Nov 2025, reporting Amnesty International 'Flooded and Forgotten'

quotes.text: Five people, including three children aged 5, 11, and 16, died in the Lamontville TRA during those floods.
The area is prone to flooding.
quotes.source: South African Weather Service forecaster, quoted in Daily Maverick, 26 Feb 2025

quotes.text: We don't have enough land to settle people. We are now appealing to amakhosi or neighbouring amakhosi to make land available.
quotes.source: eThekwini Mayor Cyril Xaba, IOL, 16 Mar 2025

quotes.text: If it rains even at night, we don't know what will happen to those left behind.
quotes.source: KZN Premier Thamsanqa Ntuli, IOL, 16 Mar 2025

cases.notes: Baseline case. The Amnesty PDF itself could not be text-extracted; Amnesty findings are taken from IOL's coverage and search snippets of the report. It is unclear whether this TRA is the same as, or adjacent to, the Gwala Street transit camp (ZA-KZN-02); both are in Lamontville near the Umlaas canal / Umlazi river. The AGSA 20% 'unsuitable land' figure covers 30 TRUs inspected across KZN and is not specific to Lamontville.

cases.place: Gwala Street transit camp, Lamontville, eThekwini (Durban), KwaZulu-Natal (near the Umlaas canal)
cases.relocation_year: Feb/March 2021 (after about two years in tents at Tehuis Hostel following the April 2019 floods)
cases.agency: eThekwini Metropolitan Municipality; residents were ordered back by the ward councillor
cases.reason_for_relocation: Residents of the Mega Village informal settlement (on the banks of the Umlaas canal, uMlazi) lost their homes in floods in 2012, 2016 and April 2019.
cases.floodprone_evidence: The camp flooded in April 2022 and residents fled to hostel community halls. The Mail & Guardian described the site as 'low-lying near the Umlaas Canal, which is prone to flooding' and built on 'saturated, flood-prone ground'. Daily Maverick reported that Eskom had marked the site as unsafe because of a high-voltage cable underneath.
cases.consequences: More than 100 people sheltered in hostel halls without water or electricity from 11 April 2022. They were then ordered to return to the damaged camp. The family had been moved four times since 2012 (GroundUp). No deaths were reported in these articles for 2022.
cases.deaths_at_site: not_found for 2022 (see ZA-KZN-01 for the Feb 2025 deaths in the Lamontville TRA)
cases.government_response: Ward 74 councillor Nolubabalo Mthembu ordered flood victims to 'return to their Lamontville transit camp'. Municipal spokesperson Msawakhe Mayisela said ablution complaints had been referred for investigation. In paraphrase (Daily Maverick opinion), he attributed flooding to illegal dumping and people building on floodplains.
cases.risk_known_before: Partly. Before the 2022 flood, Daily Maverick (23 Mar 2022) reported that Eskom officials had marked the site unsafe for habitation (electrical hazard, not flood). An assessment of flood risk before the 2021 relocation was not_found.
cases.temporary_vs_permanent: A transit camp (temporary). Residents were in tents 2019-2021 and in the camp from 2021, and were still there in 2022.
cases.distance_or_position: Low-lying ground near the Umlaas canal, above a high-voltage cable.
cases.blame_framing: Residents and dumping (paraphrase): the municipal spokesperson 'attributed flooding to illegal dumping and people building on floodplains' (Daily Maverick opinion, 2022).
cases.resident_voice: Yes. A 47-year-old grandmother (GroundUp): 'We have been moved from one place to another and we are tired now.' Shelter occupants said they 'did not have dignified, safe accommodation' (M&G).
cases.who_was_moved: Low-income, mostly unemployed former informal-settlement residents of Mega Village, uMlazi. Language or minority group: not_found.

quotes.text: We have been moved from one place to another and we are tired now.
quotes.source: Resident quoted in GroundUp, 'Some Durban flood victims have been moved four times' (2022)

quotes.text: They might return only to be swept away in the next flood, which could be next year, next month or tomorrow.

cases.notes: The M&G and Daily Maverick pieces are opinion articles, but GroundUp's news report independently confirms the moves and the 2022 flooding. This case may overlap with ZA-KZN-01; it shows the Lamontville site cluster flooded in 2022, three years before the fatal 2025 flood.

cases.place: Isipingo transit camp (Willcox Road), south Durban, eThekwini, KwaZulu-Natal
flooded_years: multiple ('four or five occasions'), including April 2022
cases.reason_for_relocation: People were cleared from informal settlements in Umlazi, the Bluff and Mayville ahead of the 2010 FIFA World Cup (Rising Sun). A DA statement says the camp was 'established ... following natural disasters in the area'.
cases.floodprone_evidence: Repeated flooding. The camp is located 'in between a river and a highway' (Rising Sun). A search-engine summary of IOL coverage said the camp 'is built in a flood plain with little drainage'; this was not verified because the IOL page returned 403.
cases.consequences: Two electrocution deaths linked to the April (2022) floods: a woman who 'tripped and fell onto a live wire while pouring out a bucket of water', and a man who died 'while trying to fix an electrical fault' the day after the floods. Residents were still in one-room structures after 13 years. There were violent protests in July 2023 over delays in moving to the Kanku Road housing project.
cases.deaths_at_site: 2 (electrocutions after April 2022 floods, per Rising Sun)
cases.government_response: Mayor Mxolisi Kaunda launched the Kanku Road Housing Project (360 units) in March 2020. It was completed in June 2023, but moves were held up by an audit.
cases.temporary_vs_permanent: Residents were promised better houses 'after six to nine months'. More than 300 families were still there after about 13-14 years.
cases.distance_or_position: Between a river and a highway; reportedly on a flood plain.
cases.resident_voice: Yes. A camp committee member: 'On four or five occasions, we have experienced flooding and our household items have been damaged by mud and water.'
cases.who_was_moved: Low-income informal-settlement residents from Umlazi, the Bluff and Mayville. Language or minority group: not_found.
cases.accountability_outcome: none found (protests; a political party statement)

quotes.text: On four or five occasions, we have experienced flooding and our household items have been damaged by mud and water
quotes.source: Isipingo camp committee member, Rising Sun Newspapers (2022)

quotes.text: This camp was established by the ANC government in 2010 following natural disasters in the area.
quotes.source: DA MP Tim Brauteseth statement, Polity, 21 Jul 2023

cases.notes: The sources disagree on the year and the reason for relocation (World Cup clearance vs natural disaster). The deaths were electrocutions during the flood aftermath, not drownings.

cases.place: Temporary residential units (TRUs) for April 2022 flood victims, KwaZulu-Natal (province-wide sample)
flooded_years: not_found (audit finding, not a flood event)
cases.agency: KZN Department of Human Settlements and contractors (TRU programme), audited by the Auditor-General of South Africa (AGSA)
cases.reason_for_relocation: Rehousing people whose homes were destroyed in the April 2022 floods.
cases.floodprone_evidence: Official audit: of 30 TRUs inspected, all failed minimum specifications and 20% had been 'constructed on unsuitable land' (AGSA first real-time audit report, August 2022). The AG noted that 'some were built on unsuitable land'. The brief describes this finding as units close to the riverbank; the sources accessed say only 'unsuitable land'.
cases.consequences: Only 736 of 1,810 planned KZN TRUs were complete by 31 July 2022. A later News24 report (May 2023) said every temporary home inspected was defective.
cases.government_response: The KZN Premier sought an urgent meeting with the AG over the findings. Parliament's committee welcomed the report.
cases.risk_known_before: yes. AGSA flagged unsuitable siting in August 2022, before the February 2025 floods.
cases.temporary_vs_permanent: Temporary. The DA estimated in October 2022 that delivery could take up to four years.
cases.distance_or_position: 'unsuitable land' (not further specified in sources accessed)
cases.who_was_moved: Flood-displaced households across KZN, largely from informal settlements.
cases.accountability_outcome: An AGSA audit and parliamentary oversight. No sanctions specific to siting were found.

quotes.text: Of the 30 that we inspected, all of them had non-compliances with minimum specifications
quotes.source: Auditor-General, quoted in Daily Maverick, 31 Aug 2022

quotes.text: Inspections of the units also revealed that some were built on unsuitable land and that some installations did not meet the agreed specifications.

cases.notes: This is an assessment case, not a single site. It shows the state's own auditor flagged siting problems in 2022. 'Unsuitable land' is not necessarily a flood hazard; do not overstate it.

cases.place: Proposed relocation site at Cullinan (near Rayton), City of Tshwane, Gauteng, for 2022 Mamelodi flood victims (e.g. from Eerste Fabriek on the Moretele River)
flooded_years: not_found (the site has not been reported as flooded)
cases.agency: Gauteng Provincial Government / City of Tshwane
cases.reason_for_relocation: Flood victims from Mamelodi informal settlements flooded in 2019 and 2022.
cases.floodprone_evidence: ALLEGED. A DA Gauteng statement (31 Mar 2025) says the site is 'on a wetland' and warns that sewage from an overloaded Rayton works could flow into the Elands River near the site. No hydrological assessment was found.
cases.consequences: Local opposition in Cullinan (Ridge Times, Jan 2025).
cases.government_response: not_found for the wetland claim. In 2022 Tshwane spokesperson Lindela Mashigo said 'The City and [Gauteng] province are currently engaging on the approach for the relocation.'
cases.risk_known_before: Alleged by an opposition party (DA, Mar 2025) before the relocation.
cases.resident_voice: Mamelodi resident (Daily Maverick, 2022): 'I live in fear whenever there is heavy rain.'

quotes.text: We are waiting for the land that they [City of Tshwane] promised us in December 2019.
quotes.source: Eerste Fabriek community leader, Daily Maverick, 2 Dec 2022

cases.notes: Only alleged, and only by a political party. The relocation is planned, not completed. Include only as a 'risk flagged before relocation' example.

cases.place: Cyclone Idai resettlement sites in Sofala (esp. Buzi, Dondo, Chibabava, Nhamatanda, Caia), Manica and Zambezia provinces
cases.agency: Government of Mozambique via INGD (National Institute for Disaster Risk Management), with IOM and humanitarian partners
cases.reason_for_relocation: Displacement by Cyclone Idai (March 2019) and floods (Dec 2019 - Feb 2020).
cases.floodprone_evidence: Later flood. Eloise damaged or destroyed shelters of at least 8,755 families living in 70 resettlement sites, 6,790 of them in Sofala; Buzi was worst hit with 4,619 households. Five sites were cut off by floodwater on 26 January 2021: Inhajou 2019, Nhamacunta and Savane (Sofala), and Tossene Choma and Ngurue (Manica). IOM said 'more than half' of the sites had 'restricted access due to flooding'.
cases.consequences: Damage to 5,292 latrines, 8 water points, 11 schools and 6 health centres at or near the sites. Renewed displacement of Idai survivors. Some families were later moved again to 'higher ground' sites (e.g. Bopira and Mussinemue in Buzi) with IOM support.
cases.government_response: INGD informed residents about flood risks and advised relocation decisions (IOM story). The New Humanitarian (2019) had reported the sites were built 'away from low-lying, flood-prone areas' but in remote settings (search-engine summary).
cases.risk_known_before: not_found (no pre-siting flood assessment located). The sites were presented as safe from flooding.
cases.temporary_vs_permanent: Resettlement sites intended as permanent; many residents still lived in emergency tents nearly two years later.
cases.distance_or_position: Various; several were reachable only across flood-prone roads.
cases.resident_voice: Resident of a later higher-ground site (IOM): 'it is higher up and already withstood the last harsh rains and storms, and it is proven to not flood.'
cases.who_was_moved: Rural and peri-urban cyclone survivors in central Mozambique, largely subsistence farmers (place-level).

quotes.text: over half of the 71 resettlement centres sheltering people displaced by the 2019 Cyclone Idai, are in areas affected by Cyclone Eloise
quotes.source: IOM spokesperson Paul Dillon, UN News, Jan 2021

cases.notes: The numbers come from the IOM/INGD Flash Report 16 as summarised in search results; the ReliefWeb page returned 403. Much of the damage was wind and rain damage to shelters, not necessarily inundation of the sites. Treat as 'resettlement sites hit and cut off by flooding', not proof that sites were sited in floodplains.

cases.place: Hopley Farm settlement (incl. Gada area), Harare
cases.agency: Government of Zimbabwe / City of Harare (Operation Garikai/Hlalani Kuhle)
cases.reason_for_relocation: Forced evictions under Operation Murambatsvina (2005). The government 'directed the City of Harare to allocate households displaced by OM plots in Hopley Farm Settlement'.
cases.floodprone_evidence: Credible assessment: houses in the Gada area are 'built in a wetland and are vulnerable to waterlogging and floods' (ICCCAD study visit). Frontiers (2022) notes a wetland at the dam area. Later flood: homes, toilets and school classrooms collapsed in the January 2017 Harare floods (GroundUp).
cases.consequences: House collapses and loss of property in 2017. No deaths reported.
cases.government_response: A Harare Town Clerk representative said the City was 'unaware that rains had damaged people's dwellings'. A City Health spokesperson ended the interview after asking: 'Who told you we ignore people affected by floods?'
cases.temporary_vs_permanent: Started as temporary accommodation for evictees (2005); it became a long-term settlement (more than 17 years).
cases.distance_or_position: Part of the settlement (Gada) is in a wetland.
cases.resident_voice: Resident (GroundUp): 'I thank God no one was inside. We could be counting bodies.'
cases.who_was_moved: Low-income urban evictees pushed out of central Harare (place-level).
cases.accountability_outcome: none found (UN criticism of Murambatsvina in general)

quotes.text: houses in Hopely Farm's Gada area that are built in a wetland and are vulnerable to waterlogging and floods
quotes.source: ICCCAD, 'Study visit to Hopley Farm in Zimbabwe'

quotes.text: the government of Zimbabwe directed the City of Harare to allocate households displaced by OM plots in Hopley Farm Settlement
Who told you we ignore people affected by floods?
quotes.source: City of Harare Health Department spokesperson, GroundUp, Jan 2017

cases.notes: An eviction-then-flood case. It is not established that the specific plots allocated by the state are the ones that flooded. Many residents later settled informally.

cases.place: IDP camps in Dikwa LGA, Borno State (and Maiduguri camps such as El Miskin, Muna)
cases.agency: not_found for camp siting. Camps are administered under Borno State authorities with humanitarian partners (not verified in sources accessed).
cases.reason_for_relocation: Displacement by the insurgency in north-east Nigeria.
cases.floodprone_evidence: Later flood. Overflow of the Alau Dam and the Yadzaram River flooded 12 IDP camps in Dikwa, five of them completely submerged, affecting 24,676 people (3,907 households). El Miskin camp (about 7,000 IDPs) in Maiduguri was also reportedly flooded.
cases.consequences: More than 27,000 people displaced again in Dikwa. 373 latrines and 8 water points damaged. Flood-displaced people in Maiduguri were moved into the former Bakassi IDP camp, which was already full.
cases.government_response: The federal and state governments reopened closed IDP camps as relocation sites for flood victims (Channels TV, Gavi).
cases.temporary_vs_permanent: IDP camps (temporary), in use for years
cases.distance_or_position: Downstream of the Alau Dam / near the Yadzaram River
cases.notes: The figures come from OCHA documents as summarised in search results (the pages returned 403), so no verbatim quote was captured. Who chose the camp sites was not documented.

cases.place: Bentiu IDP camp (former UNMISS Protection of Civilians site), Rubkona County, Unity State
cases.relocation_year: from 2013-2014 (conflict); flood-displaced people also moved into the camp area after 2020
cases.agency: UNMISS (camp origin); Government of Unity State with IOM, UNMISS and WFP (dykes and response)
cases.reason_for_relocation: Civil war displacement, then floods from 2020 that 'have never fully receded'.
cases.floodprone_evidence: Officially acknowledged. The camp sits on 'a tiny sliver of land surrounded by 4,500 square kilometres of floodwater' and depends on dykes built in 2021 with the Government of South Sudan. The main dyke broke in October 2022 and part of the camp was submerged.
cases.consequences: The camp was cut off from Rubkona and Bentiu. The state minister said about 100 people were displaced within the camp in the Oct 2022 breach. Around 109,000-112,000 people remain at ongoing risk.
cases.government_response: Dyke construction and reinforcement with IOM and partners. The State Information Minister downplayed the October 2022 breach.
cases.risk_known_before: yes. Floods since 2020 and dykes built in 2021, before the 2022 breach.
cases.temporary_vs_permanent: An emergency protection site that has lasted about a decade.
cases.distance_or_position: Surrounded by floodwater; below the dyke line.
cases.blame_framing: Minimisation: 'there are not too many populated people who have displaced'.
cases.resident_voice: IDPs described the water buildup as 'alarming' (Eye Radio).
cases.who_was_moved: Conflict- and flood-displaced people of Unity State (place-level).

quotes.text: so there are not too many populated people who have displaced it maybe a hundred people who have been displaced yesterday because of dyke in IDP camp yesterday.
quotes.source: Unity State Information Minister David Gai Jiejor, Eye Radio, Oct 2022

cases.notes: The camp was founded by the UN mission, not the government, so it fits the 'government-contracted agency' criterion only partly. The 4,500 km2 figure comes from a search-engine summary of UN/UNHCR pages.

cases.place: IDP gathering sites and reception centres, Kassala town and Gharb Kassala, Kassala State
cases.agency: not_found (gathering sites are typically designated by state authorities; not verified)
cases.floodprone_evidence: Later flood: five gathering sites and reception centres were hit by 118 mm of rain on 25-26 July 2024, affecting more than 10,000 IDPs.
cases.consequences: Many IDPs forced to 'live in the open along roadsides'. About 500 family tents were set up at the West Airport gathering site for people flooded out of the Al Sinaya reception centre.
cases.notes: The sites flooded, but there is no evidence that the sites were known to be flood-prone or that the government chose them. Included for completeness.

screened_out.place: Blikkiesdorp (Symphony Way TRA), Delft, Cape Town
screened_out.reason: Sewage overflows and ponding when it rains are documented, but no source found showing the TRA flooded or was assessed as flood-prone.
Isolation, fire and overcrowding are documented, but no flooding.
Floods badly (Kuils River), but it was formed by land occupation, not relocation.
Community opposition was about crime, not flood risk.
A counter-example: the site was assessed as geologically safe by ZINGSA, but residents face drought and water scarcity instead.
No flooding of the new site reported, though children must cross rivers to reach school.
Evictions without relocation; a High Court ordered compensation. No state relocation into a flood-prone site found.
Dam-flood victims were relocated there under coercive conditions (HRW), but no flooding of the camp itself was found.

screened_out.place: Lagos (Makoko/Otodo Gbame), Accra (Old Fadama), Derna (Libya), Barwaaqo/Baidoa (Somalia)
screened_out.reason: No documented case of state relocation into a site that then flooded was found in this search.

patterns_observed: 'Temporary' becomes permanent: sites announced as transit camps or TRAs held people for 3 years (Lamontville TRA), 13-14 years (Isipingo), about 17 years (eMhlabeni) and more than 17 years (Hopley). Exposure grows the longer people stay.

Serial displacement in the same flood corridor: Durban households moved from Mega Village (flooded 2012, 2016, 2019) to Tehuis tents, then to a Lamontville camp that flooded in 2022, then to a Lamontville TRA where five people died in 2025. All of these sites are within the Umlaas canal / Umlazi river system.

The risk was visible before the deaths: the camp flooded in April 2022 and this was reported in national media, and the AGSA flagged TRUs on unsuitable land in August 2022, almost three years before the fatal February 2025 flood.

Land scarcity is the main official justification ('We don't have enough land'; 'we do not have land that is available'), along with neighbour opposition in better-off areas (Umhlanga, Cullinan, Maydene Farm).

Blame falls on weather and climate ('unprecedented rainfall') or on residents (dumping, building on floodplains), rather than on how the sites were chosen. No official acceptance of responsibility was found in any case.

Accountability is weak: no inquiries, court rulings, resignations or compensation tied to site choice were found. Scrutiny came from the AGSA, Amnesty International, journalists and opposition parties.
Warnings are generic: SAWS issued a regional Yellow Level 2 warning, but no source documented a warning reaching TRA residents or the language it was in. This is a gap to investigate.
Secondary hazards: at Isipingo the post-flood deaths were electrocutions from illegal connections, and Lamontville's camp sat above a high-voltage cable. Poor servicing turns floods deadlier.

Across Africa, camps and resettlement sites for conflict or disaster survivors (Mozambique Idai sites, Dikwa, Bentiu, Kassala) repeatedly flood. Documented pre-siting hydrological assessments are rare; the exception found is a geological (not flood) screening at Runyararo, Zimbabwe.
Those moved are consistently low-income informal-settlement dwellers or evictees, relocated to the urban periphery or to leftover, low-lying land.
